job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — 10,000-ton threshold.** The bill affirmatively permits recovery of up to and including 10,000 metric tons per year, which is a substantial commercial operation. A prohibition should not depend on exceeding a production threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel calculation.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” an operator could divide production among multiple vessels, each recovering no more than 10,000 tons. Production should be aggregated across affiliated persons, vessels, equipment, and projects.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Operations that do not use a vessel.** Fixed platforms, subsea equipment, autonomous vehicles, pipelines, and other systems might recover minerals without recovery being attributable to a “single vessel.” The definition should cover projects and operations regardless of the technology used.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Per year” is undefined.** The bill does not say whether this means a calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or rolling 12-month period. An operator could exploit this ambiguity by splitting a large operation across reporting periods.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Violation begins only after the threshold is crossed.** It is unclear whether an operation becomes unlawful only upon recovery of ton 10,001 and whether penalties can apply to activities conducted earlier in the year. This would make timely injunctions and enforcement before extraction difficult.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Measurement is unspecified.** The text does not state whether tonnage is measured as wet material, dry material, ore, concentrate, or contained minerals, or at what point “recovery” occurs. Different measurement methods could determine whether an operation falls under the Act.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** Companies could argue that collection, excavation, pumping, lifting, testing, storage, or preliminary processing is not “recovery.” The bill should expressly cover prospecting and exploration activities that disturb the seabed, extraction, collection, lifting, transport, and processing at sea.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth boundary and measurement.** Activity at exactly 200 meters is excluded, and the bill does not specify how depth is measured or account for varying tides and seabed topography. The chosen depth also sweeps in some relatively shallow national waters while potentially failing to track the intended concept of the “deep seabed.”

9. **Section 2(1)(A) — Geographic scope is unclear.** “The seabed” is not defined, so it is uncertain whether the bill covers the U.S. continental shelf, foreign national waters, and the international seabed Area equally. If the objective is to cover all deep-seabed mining by U.S. actors, that scope should be stated expressly.

10. **Section 2(1)(A) — Minerals and ecosystems are undefined.** “Other mineral resources” and “deep-sea ecosystems” have no definitions, creating uncertainty about deposits such as seafloor massive sulfides, cobalt-rich crusts, and minerals beneath rather than lying on the seabed.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unidentified Secretary.** The Act never defines “the Secretary,” so no official is clearly empowered to make the determination in subparagraph (B). Section 6’s separate reference to the Secretary of State makes the ambiguity more pronounced.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — Discretionary, reactive coverage.** The Secretary “determines” which other activities pose comparable risks, but has no duty or deadline to do so. A novel mining technique may therefore remain outside the prohibition until an affirmative determination is completed.

13. **Section 2(1)(B) — No standards or procedure.** “Risks … comparable” supplies no methodology, factors, evidentiary standard, rulemaking procedure, or definition of the relevant risk. That invites vagueness and delegation challenges and makes determinations easier to contest.

14. **Section 2(2) — Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition omits U.S. nationals, permanent residents, partnerships, LLCs, associations, trusts, unincorporated entities, District of Columbia and territorial entities, and corporations organized under federal law. It also does not expressly include government instrumentalities.

15. **Section 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries and control arrangements.** A U.S. company could conduct mining through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary, joint venture, nominee, or contractor. The definition should address ownership, control, beneficial ownership, and conduct performed on behalf of a U.S. person.

16. **Sections 2 and 3 — “Person” is not defined.** Section 3 applies to “any person,” but the Act defines only “U.S. person.” Although the Dictionary Act may supply a default, an express definition would avoid disputes and should include entities, responsible officers, affiliates, agents, and successors.

17. **Section 2(3) — Vessel-tonnage loophole.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons and all smaller vessels are excluded from the registry even if they can conduct significant mining. Operators could also distribute equipment among several smaller vessels.

18. **Section 2(3) — Narrow and ambiguous vessel coverage.** “Equipped for the recovery” may exclude support, survey, processing, storage, transport, and command vessels, as well as vessels carrying modular or temporarily removed equipment. “Gross tons” should also identify the applicable vessel-measurement convention.

19. **Section 3(a) — “Engage in” is undefined.** The prohibition may not reach financing, insuring, investing in, authorizing, directing, facilitating, contracting for, processing, purchasing, or transporting minerals from a mining operation. It also does not expressly prohibit attempts, conspiracy, aiding and abetting, or causing a violation.

20. **Section 3(a) — Territorial wording is ambiguous.** “Any person in the United States” can be read as turning on where the person is located rather than where the conduct occurs. The bill should separately address conduct within U.S. territory or jurisdiction, conduct using U.S.-flagged vessels, and conduct abroad by covered U.S. actors.

21. **Section 3(a) — U.S.-flagged vessels and other U.S. jurisdictional links.** A foreign operator using a U.S.-flagged vessel abroad may not be a “U.S. person” and may not be “in the United States.” Aircraft, ports, financing systems, and equipment subject to U.S. jurisdiction are likewise not expressly covered.

22. **Section 3(a) — Existing permitting laws are not reconciled.** The bill does not repeal, suspend, or bar issuance and transfer of licenses and permits under existing deep-seabed mining statutes or other federal authorities. Companies could argue that existing statutory rights or agency authorities survive, producing conflicting legal regimes.

23. **Section 3(b) — Undefined “exploration license.”** The text does not say which government or body must have issued the license, potentially recognizing licenses from foreign states, the International Seabed Authority, subnational bodies, or an unauthorized issuer.

24. **Section 3(b) — Exploration license becomes a mining exemption.** The provision exempts “mining conducted under an exploration license,” allowing a pre-enactment exploration authorization to serve as a grandfathered commercial mining right. It contains no production cap, environmental conditions, geographic limit, or requirement that mining was already occurring.

25. **Section 3(b) — Unlimited grandfathering and transfers.** The exemption has no expiration, review, revocation, anti-expansion, or anti-transfer provision. It could cover expired, renewed, amended, assigned, or substantially expanded licenses and could outlast the original licensee.

26. **Section 3(c) — Environmental-assessment pretext.** Coverage turns on an operator’s claimed “purpose,” with no approval, scientific protocol, quantity limit, independent oversight, or requirement that disturbance be necessary and minimized. A company could characterize extraction or equipment trials as environmental assessment.

27. **Section 3(c) — Mixed-purpose activities.** The bill does not address activities having both assessment and commercial, exploration, or technology-demonstration purposes. Even incidental sale or retention of recovered minerals is not prohibited.

28. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, bareboat charter, technical management, remote control, and operational control may rest with different parties. Without a definition and joint responsibility, each could argue that another entity had the registration duty.

29. **Section 4(a) — No registration deadline or implementing mechanism.** The bill does not say when, how, or with what information a vessel must register, and it gives NOAA no express rulemaking authority. It also appears to demand registration of every covered vessel worldwide without limiting the requirement to persons or vessels within U.S. jurisdiction.

30. **Section 4 — Registry evasion.** Registration applies only to “covered vessels,” while the substantive prohibition can apply more broadly. Smaller vessels and non-vessel systems therefore produce no registry or reports, weakening detection of unlawful mining.

31. **Section 4(b) — Inadequate reporting requirements.** “Describing the recovery activities” does not require location, dates, quantities, mineral type, equipment, ownership, customers, environmental effects, or supporting records. The provision also lacks record-retention, audit, inspection, public-disclosure, and electronic-reporting requirements.

32. **Sections 4 and 5 — No penalty for registry or reporting violations.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failure to register, failure to report, late reporting, and inaccurate reporting are therefore not expressly enforceable under this Act.

33. **Section 5(a) — No designated enforcement authority or process.** The bill does not identify the agency or Attorney General responsible for investigations, assessment or collection of penalties, administrative hearings, judicial actions, or appeals. It also supplies no subpoena, inspection, monitoring, or information-demand authority.

34. **Section 5(a) — Penalty may be nominal.** “Not more than” $1 million supplies a ceiling but no minimum or mandatory factors, allowing a penalty of zero or an amount lower than the profits from mining. There is no adjustment for inflation, disgorgement, remediation, or per-vessel, per-ton, or per-act penalty.

35. **Section 5 — Missing enforcement remedies.** The bill does not expressly authorize injunctions, emergency cease-and-desist orders, vessel detention, permit revocation, forfeiture of vessels or minerals, restoration, response-cost recovery, or citizen suits. Monetary penalties imposed after extraction may not prevent irreversible harm.

36. **Section 5(b) — Difficult criminal intent standard.** “Willfully” may require proof that a defendant knew the conduct was unlawful, creating a demanding burden where the Act’s definitions are ambiguous. There are no separate offenses for knowing evasion, concealment, false reporting, or obstruction.

37. **Sections 5(a) and 8 — Conflicting penalty and effective dates.** Section 5 applies to violations “on or after the date of enactment,” but section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. This creates uncertainty over whether section 3 applies immediately for penalty purposes or only after 180 days.

38. **Section 6 — Merely aspirational international mandate.** Requiring the Secretary of State to “seek to negotiate” does not require negotiations to begin, an agreement to be concluded, or any result to be reported to Congress. “Equivalent” prohibitions could also reproduce all of section 3’s thresholds and exemptions rather than establish a comprehensive international ban.

39. **Section 7(a) — No mechanism for the National Academies report.** The bill neither directs nor funds the National Academies to prepare a report and sets no standards, scope, peer-review requirements, or deadline. Congress could therefore lack the report contemplated by the provision, or rely on one not designed to answer the statutory question.

40. **Section 7(a) — Undefined reopening standard.** “Without serious harm” does not define the relevant ecosystems, time horizon, cumulative effects, evidentiary burden, or required degree of scientific certainty. That ambiguity could allow reopening despite substantial or irreversible harm.

41. **Section 7(a) — Joint-resolution mechanics are incomplete.** The bill does not specify the text, procedures, presidential presentment, or effective date of the contemplated joint resolution. It also says the prohibition lasts until Congress “finds” the condition satisfied, rather than clearly requiring enactment of a law terminating the prohibition.

42. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b) — Internal contradiction.** Subsection (a) suggests the prohibition continues unless Congress affirmatively determines mining is safe, but subsection (b) automatically terminates the entire Act after 10 years regardless of harm or scientific evidence. The sunset defeats the precautionary structure of subsection (a).

43. **Section 7(b) — Sunset eliminates more than the prohibition.** Because “this Act” ceases to have effect, the registry, reporting obligations, penalties, and international-negotiation mandate also disappear. If any continuing review is intended after ten years, the text does not preserve it.

44. **Section 7(b) — No savings clause.** The bill does not preserve liabilities, pending enforcement cases, reporting duties, or remedies for violations committed before sunset. Defendants could invoke the expiration to argue that pending civil or criminal proceedings abate.

45. **Section 8 — Unclear treatment of the 180-day interim.** The bill neither bars agencies from issuing, renewing, or transferring mining authorizations during the delay nor requires companies to wind down preparations. Operators could use the period to obtain licenses that they later claim fall within section 3(b), although that exemption uses the earlier enactment-date cutoff.
